messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I conducted line transect distance sampling for mammalian species in a nature reserve. Since most species were in low density, I only managed to have one species that seems to have large enough sampling size for analysis in the program.
I am a newbie in R and Distance, and i would like to have some advice for you

(1) My data have quite a lot of Zero Sighting distance, as most of the animals were seen on the transect itself (i think it is the nature of the animals that they like to use the road system to travel within the reserve), i wonder if this will affect the analysis and if there is any transformation needed before the analysis
I try to run the data according to the example in "montrave robin example" but it seems that the data just doesnt fit in the model, (most have highly significant P-value and data points were far off from the goodness of fit ...)

(2)Did i miss anything or the sample size is still to small to run the analysis? Or it is just that this data just couldnt be analysed using Distance??? If so , do you have any suggestions what program i could use?

I am stuck at the moment and unsure what to do next. I have attached the data file and the steps that i did for the analysis.

Any advice would be useful !! Much thanks!!

Best,
Tamari

Hi Distance users,

I have a query relating to the number of observations (n) output in the detection function summary in R. Both cds and mrds model outputs have less observations than exist in my actual dataset (just a couple out of ~100 detections are missing). At first I thought this was an error and have been checking my tables and data types in R to see if there is a mistake somewhere. However I’ve come across Dave Miller’s ‘Distance sampling in R’ webpage where the wording is ‘The summary tells us how many observations were used to fit the data’. This suggests that it might be possible that the model does not use all the data to fit it. Could someone confirm if it normal that a few detections are not included in the model fit? For the cds analysis where I have used a flatfile and therefore get subsequent abundance estimates directly from the model, I suppose this means that not all observations were in included in the final count?

Many thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Tamari

The document you provided describing your analysis is very clear.  You have drawn the correct conclusion that because > half of your detections are recorded at distance 0 from the transect, you cannot fit a reasonable detection function to the data:
> tamari <- read.csv(file.choose())
> sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(tamari$distance))
[1] 65
> sum(tamari$distance==0, na.rm=TRUE)
[1] 33

As you note your study organism likes to use the same roads that you used for your sampling.  This violates the design assumption of distance sampling.  Transects should be placed randomly in the landscape and roads are not placed randomly.  Equally important, there should be as many animals in the strip, say between 10 and 11m from the  transect as are located between 0 and 1m from the transect.  Another way of saying this is animals should not know where the transects are located (and either avoid or gravitate toward the transects).

There really is not a remedy to apply during the analysis.  The better solution is a re-design of your survey so as to produce random placement of transects throughout the study area.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about an issue I've experienced with stratifying versus filtering my data in program Distance.

Research summary:
I am trying to obtain abundance estimates of grassland bird species before and after bison reintroduction and between bison-grazed, cattle-grazed, and reference (no cattle or bison) treatments. I conducted point count surveys at 20 point count stations within each treatment. I had three field seasons from May-June 2015, 2016, and 2017. Within each season, I visited each point count station 5 times. For my first analysis, I would like to compare abundance between years (before and after bison reintroduction) and between only the bison and reference treatments .

Analysis issue:
I am performing a Half-normal Cosine, MCDS analysis with covariates that include observer, wind, rain, and cloud cover. For my most observed species (>100 observations per treatment included in analysis after truncation), when I stratify by treatment (bison or reference) in the "Model Definition" window and place covariates on detection probability, program Distance cannot estimate abundance for the reference site. I get a zero for abundance, and do not get an estimate of the effective detection radius or detection probability for the reference site. However, when I filter by treatment in the "Data Filter" window, I am able to place covariates on detection probability and get results for the reference site.

Why would I be able to filter the data by treatment but not stratify the data by treatment?

Thanks so much for any insights on this!

Best,
Kate

messages.body_plain:
Kate

Sounds like an interesting experiment.  I'll make several comments.

Your inclusion of four covariates are likely causing you difficulty.  You aren't explicit, but I suspect most or all of the covariates are factor rather than continuous.  If they are all factors, then you should query your data to discover how many detections you have in each of the possible categories of covariates.  Pretend you have but two levels for each of your covariates--that results in 2^4 different combinations (16).  That shrinks your 100 observations per treatment down to ~8 detections per combination (assuming all combinations are equally represented).  That will make for a challenging parameter estimation problem.

However, the situation is likely not that rosy.  There are likely combinations that have no detections (presence of rain in the absence of cloud cover); that make the estimation problem even more difficult (likely leading to convergence failure in the estimation routine).  To top it off, your covariates are likely collinear (correlation between your meteorological variables).  You are also incorporating adjustment terms along with the covariates.  Not a surprise that you suffer failure of model fitting.

I suggest you work with a less ambitious models.  There is a section in the users guide called "MCDS analysis guidelines" that discusses these difficulties.  In part, here is a portion of that section:

Fitting the detection function with multiple covariates is significantly harder, computationally, than in the case where there is only one covariate.  This has
several consequences:
• the analysis engine takes longer to run
• the algorithm will fail to converge more often
Because of this, it is important to be careful and thoughtful when setting up and running MCDS analyses.  Here are some recommendations:
• Rather than including numerous covariates at once, start by including one covariate at a time, and selecting the covariate that gives the best model fit/lowest AIC/AICc/BIC. You can then carry out forward stepwise selection by adding one additional covariate at a time, while retaining the one(s) already selected, until there is no decrease in the AIC/AICc/BIC value (depending on the criteria you are using).
• Bear in mind that factor covariates are usually harder to fit than non-factor covariates, especially as the number of factor levels increases (see Factor and Non-factor Covariates in MCDS earlier in this Chapter for information on factor covariates). If you encounter problems while trying to fit a factor covariate, try reducing (condensing) its number of levels, if possible.
• Avoid using the feature that allows automatic selection of adjustment terms – at least to start with.  Instead, start by using a model with no adjustments, and if this converges try one with one adjustment.  Gradually work up to more adjustments if required.

Two final thoughts.  Recognise distance sampling has the property of pooling robustness--meaning abundance estimates are unbiased even when all forms of heterogeneity in detection probability are not modelled.  Another reason to simplify the detection function model.  Lastly, you note you are still in the preliminary states of your analysis, have a look at this paper
Buckland, Stephen T., Robin E. Russell, Brett G. Dickson, Victoria A. Saab, Donal N. Gorman, and William M. Block. 2009. “Analyzing Designed Experiments in Distance Sampling.” Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics 14 (4):432–42. https://doi.org/10.1198/jabes.2009.08030.

for a situation perhaps similar to yours.

That will make for a challenging parameter estimation problem.

There are likely combinations that have no detections (presence of rain in the absence of cloud cover); that make the estimation problem even more difficult (likely leading to convergence failure in the estimation routine).  To top it off, your covariates are likely collinear (correlation between your meteorological variables).  You are also incorporating adjustment terms along with the covariates.  Not a surprise that you suffer failure of model fitting.
>
> I suggest you work with a less ambitious models.  There is a section in the users guide called "MCDS analysis guidelines" that discusses these difficulties.  In part, here is a portion of that section:
>
> Fitting the detection function with multiple covariates is significantly harder, computationally, than in the case where there is only one covariate.  This has
> several consequences:
> • the analysis engine takes longer to run
> • the algorithm will fail to converge more often
> Because of this, it is important to be careful and thoughtful when setting up and running MCDS analyses.  Here are some recommendations:
> • Rather than including numerous covariates at once, start by including one covariate at a time, and selecting the covariate that gives the best model fit/lowest AIC/AICc/BIC. You can then carry out forward stepwise selection by adding one additional covariate at a time, while retaining the one(s) already selected, until there is no decrease in the AIC/AICc/BIC value (depending on the criteria you are using).
> • Bear in mind that factor covariates are usually harder to fit than non-factor covariates, especially as the number of factor levels increases (see Factor and Non-factor Covariates in MCDS earlier in this Chapter for information on factor covariates). If you encounter problems while trying to fit a factor covariate, try reducing (condensing) its number of levels, if possible.

Study design:
I conducted point count surveys at three different treatments (bison, cattle, and ungrazed) across three different seasons (May-June 2015, 2016, 2017). I have 20 point count stations at each treatment, and visited each point count station 5 times within a season. I collected data in 5-minute intervals, and denoted the minute in which I heard or saw a bird. The covariates I collected include continous covariates (exact distances, cloud cover, vegetation height, and vegetation cover) and categorical covariates (wind, rain, observer). The bird species I am having trouble with is Western Meadowlarks. This is a loud bird that was most often detected around 100m or greater (see graph of detection probability attached). I have not been able to fit any models to this data. My p-value for the K-S goodness of fit test is usually around 0.003.

My question is whether anyone has advice on how to deal with data on loud birds heard at far distances. This article stated that occupancy anlayses might work better for loud birds. However, when I conducted occupancy analysis for Western Meadowlarks, occupancy was 1 across all sites. With the large number of detections for Western Meadowlarks, I feel like I should be able to conduct analyses of abundance, so any advice on how best to proceed with this would be much appreciated!

Best,
Kate

messages.subject_clean: Height from ground when distance sampling arboreal wildlife
messages.body_plain:
Discussion of primate distance sampling (e.g. Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates, Buckland et al. 2010) talks about ‘animal-to-observer’ distances, used to calculate perpendicular distances used in analysis. For arboreal primates, does it not make more sense that distances to a point on the ground (or at observer's height if not on flat ground) below the animal or geometric center of the cluster should be measured, rather than to the individual or cluster spotted in a line-of-sight manner?

If not, this would seem to invalidate the assumption of detecting all individuals/clusters on the line (there would be no individuals/cluster on the line, as they would all be a minimum distance away from the observer of their height from the ground). I have not found any mention of accounting for height in core texts, but presumably either the angle from ground to animal or an estimate of the height could be recorded, then either trigonometry or Pythagoras used to calculate the distance between the observer and the animal/cluster at height 0m, then used to calculate the perpendicular distance (at height 0) from the line transect.

For example, if an animal was recorded 90 degrees from the transect and 30 meters from observer to animal (line of sight, in tree), and at a height of 20 meters, the distance from observer to the animal's location at height 0m is 22.3 meters, resulting in perpendicular distance estimates of 30 meters or 22.3 meters. The bias in this greatest close to the line and lowest furthest from the line, and consistent at varying angles.

Practical guides to primate distance sampling I have seen use simplistic illustrations collapsed to 2D (e.g. http://www.teamnetwork.org/files/protocols/primate/TEAMPrimates-PT-EN-1.0.pdf page 10). A similar dimensional collapse in the field is to extrapolate the position of the animal/cluster to height 0m, but this is never explicitly discussed in guides I have read, yet obviously no one records a primate 0 meters from the line and 30 meters up as a perpendicular distance of 30 meters! Perhaps it is something so obvious that it is rarely made explicit and I'm a pedant, but I can imagine instances of confusion, especially when using range finders (which are often easiest to point at the location of the animal/cluster rather than the ground which may be obscured by undergrowth), and with terminology like 'animal-to-observer'.

Have I misunderstood the theory? Or is the ultimate bias unimportant or accounted for in a way I've missed?

On a related but slightly different side, is there not an argument for a 3-dimensional detection function when surveying a 3-dimensional area like a forest? An observer is less likely to detect an animal 10 meters away and 50 meters up than they are to detect an animal 10 meters away at eye height.

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Olly Griffin
Sent: 12 January 2018 03:58
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] Height from ground when distance sampling arboreal wildlife

Discussion of primate distance sampling (e.g. Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates, Buckland et al. 2010) talks about ‘animal-to-observer’ distances, used to calculate perpendicular distances used in analysis. For arboreal primates, does it not make more sense that distances to a point on the ground (or at observer's height if not on flat ground) below the animal or geometric center of the cluster should be measured, rather than to the individual or cluster spotted in a line-of-sight manner?

‘Animal-to-observer’ distances are generally taken to be the horizontal distance between animal and observer, not the line-of-sight distance.

If not, this would seem to invalidate the assumption of detecting all individuals/clusters on the line (there would be no individuals/cluster on the line, as they would all be a minimum distance away from the observer of their height from the ground).

You would have to use three-dimensional distance sampling methods, if you were to use the line-of-sight distances.  The complication with that is that, while we can place samplers (lines or points) at random to ensure that on average, animal locations are independent of sampler locations, we cannot do this in the vertical dimension, so the vertical distribution of animals must be modelled.  I have not seen this done for forest surveys, but it has been done for marine surveys (e.g. Cox, M.J., Borchers, D.L., Demer, D.A., Cutter, G.R. and Brierley, A.S. (2011). Estimating Antarctic krill (Eupausia superba) density from multibeam echosounder observations using distance sampling methods. Applied Statistics 60: 301-316.)

Another option is to use horizontal distances, and estimate prob of detection at the point or on the line, rather than assume this probability is one.  E.g. use the mrds engine in Distance with double-observer data.

I have not found any mention of accounting for height in core texts, but presumably either the angle from ground to animal or an estimate of the height could be recorded, then either trigonometry or Pythagoras used to calculate the distance between the observer and the animal/cluster at height 0m, then used to calculate the perpendicular distance (at height 0) from the line transect.

Some laser rangefinders will give you both distances and the angle.  Often, detections are aural, in which case the observer is making a judgement of where the animal is.  A laser rangefinder might then be used to measure to that location, or to a point at a similar distance from the observer that is visible.

For example, if an animal was recorded 90 degrees from the transect and 30 meters from observer to animal (line of sight, in tree), and at a height of 20 meters, the distance from observer to the animal's location at height 0m is 22.3 meters, resulting in perpendicular distance estimates of 30 meters or 22.3 meters. The bias in this greatest close to the line and lowest furthest from the line, and consistent at varying angles.

Thanks for sending along your detection function curve for your meadowlarks.  Is the graph you provided for all years and treatments combined?  You note that there are >1000 observations in this analysis; that amount of data will flag fairly minute discrepancies as lack of fit.  It might be more informative to have a look at the probability detection function curve produced by Distance when analysing point transect data.

However, from looking at the data you provided, it does appear that detectability is high out to 100m; perhaps a hazard rate key function (with a flatter shoulder) might be the preferable model.  It might well be the case that the small p-values are the result of rounding of distances to favoured values (100, 150, perhaps 75?).  You might bin your data for the chi-square goodness of fit test being cognisant of these favoured distances and examine the resulting GOF results to assess whether lack of fit might be a result of rounding distance measurements.

It may be the case that taking these steps in your analysis, the goodness of fit might not be so bad.

>

Giles

A few general comments, then to your specific questions:

- Left-truncation of distance sampling data is troublesome; it is the shape of the detection function at very small distances that are central to estimating the fundamental parameters in distance sampling (f(0) for lines, h(0) for points).

- The tables you provide are a good summary of the analyses you performed; the delta-AIC values would have made a useful contribution to the tables, but for the most part that can be deduced by the information you provided.

- To assess fit for point transect data, the probability density function graphs, rather than the detection probability graphs you provided may be more useful.

Your specific questions:

- blackcap: goodness of fit tests (chisquare, KS, CvM tests) are not really used for model selection.  The strategy is to apply models and determine whether they fit--i.e. produce p-values larger than 0.05.  All the models in your blackcap table meet this criterion.  The next step is then to examine delta-AIC scores to select the model most applicable.  In this case, M6 and M7 have different truncation - hence different data; and delta-AIC cannot be used to compare them.  You then use other assessments, visual assessment of agreement between data and probability density function to make your assessment.  In the end, you will note there is little difference in the 95% confidence interval estimates for M6 and M7, so it may be a distinction without a difference.

- chaffinch: note the trivial difference in the CI bounds for S4 and S4-2.  Both treatments of the data produce models that fit the data, and very similar estimates.

- yellowhammer: I don't know what model you have shown in the figure on page 6, but that figure suggests the fitted model is not trying to fit the surplus of detections at small distances.  The question to ask is what causes the large number of detections at those small distances.  This is less a statistical modelling issue than the reason for that rapid drop in numbers of detections at roughly 35m.  I suspect had you shown estimates from hazard rate models they would have produced much larger estimates than the uniform/half-normal key functions.

Hello -

Just a quick update for anyone who is interested in post-stratification using more than one variable.  I ended up creating a new Region.Label field that included both my stand information and time period information as Dave suggested.  For example,  one of my study timber stands was called SRSFC1 and I was looking at two different time periods (pre-harvest and post-harvest), so I assigned the study stand SRSFC1 two region labels - SRSFC1_Pre and SRSFC1_Post.  I also had to update the Sample.Label field to reflect the new Region.Labels.  Area did not have to be adjusted but I did have to make sure that I divided up the Effort information to reflect the number of times that I visited SRSFC1 before logging and after logging occurred.

Once the data was restructured I was able to use the abundance estimate function in R to get estimates for each study stand pre- and post-harvest:

abundance_estimate(amro_hn, ~Region.Label)

Hope this is helpful.

Leah

messages.subject_clean: Distance in R - comparison of pooled CDS, stratified CDS and MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I am working with some bird point count data collected in binned distances. There are a total of 12 sites, 3 in each of 4 forest age classes. I would like to find out if there are differences in detectability between the age classes. I am using the package ‘Distance’ in R.

I have some queries and concerns, and would really appreciate some guidance:

Q1. I have attempted to use the “gof_ds” call to test for model fit. However, there are generally only two outcomes. Sometimes I get p-values of 0, does this suggest that fits are very poor? Alternatively, I get “No degrees of freedom for test”, presumably because there are a lot of parameters in my models. Is it still legitimate to continue with the distance sampling process if I can’t test for model fit? (I think that it means that I can’t know if the AIC selection is choosing a model with poorer fit, is that right?)

Q2. I have been following the approach of the Marques et al. (2007) Amakihi paper, i.e. I have conducted pooled CDS, stratified CDS, and MCDS. In Table 2 (p.1239) of their paper, Marques et al. present a combined summary of the model selection. How are they able to report a single combined model selection for the stratified analyses, when they have stratified their data by 7 time periods? I have done this for the 4 forest age classes, and so I have four sets of model selections, with different models selected for each age class. How could I combine these into a single selection procedure? (And would that even make sense, given that different models are selected for different age classes?)

Q3. In addition, in Table 2, Marques et al. compare all of the models for both pooled and stratified analyses, when presumably the models are based on different data (i.e. the full dataset for pooled CDS and MCDS, but only subsets for the stratified CDS). Is that correct? And if so, does this not matter? I think that I must have misunderstood their approach, but I don’t know which aspects I am failing to get my head around.

Q4. Leaving aside the issue with the stratified analyses, I have tried model selection with just the pooled CDS and the MCDS with forest age as a covariate. (I have also tried individual sites as well, but I haven't combined forest age and site because I assume that they will be correlated). In Marques et al., the MCDS models have lower AICs than the pooled CDS models, so the former are preferred. However, it is the opposite in my model selection process. The pooled CDS is chosen over the MCDS (see table below). Does this mean that the forest age covariate is not improving model fit? And therefore I can conclude that there are similar levels of detectability between forest age classes? Although I also note that the preferred models have a lot of adjustments in them, and that the model with Forest.Age as a covariate is simpler. Dear Distance users,

I have a multi-species dataset and I pooled three species that look quite similar from the aircraft (thus I expect them having similar detection functions) to build series of detection models using MRDS engine. I chose the best of them and wanted to use it in the DSM analyses to model density distribution of each of those species separately.

** Error: You are not using the same data filter for this DSM analysis (Analysis ID 341) as you are for the detection function analysis (Analysis ID 235) you have chosen to pair it with in the DSM Model Definition.  **

The data filters I want to use for DSM analyses are narrower than the one I used to build the detection model (e.g.  Species IN ('Buccla', 'Mermer', 'Aytful') in the MRDS analysis vs Species='Buccla'. in DSM). Is there a way to overcome this?  Or the only option is to build separate detection functions for each species?

Carter

Welcome to the list.

You will enter study area size, transects and associated detections into Distance--examples of line transect project organisation can be found in the Sample Projects folder after installation of Distance; e.g. "Line Transect Example.dst".  Analysis of those data will provide an estimate of nest density.  To convert from nest density to orangutan density, you will need to provide estimates of nest production rate and nest decay rate (along with measures of precision of both) are added to the Distance project with what are called multipliers.

When you create a new Distance project, the software will ask whether you wish to provide multipliers and you will be presented with this screen that I have partially completed indicating this is an indirect survey of nests--whereby the software creates four new fields in the global layer of the project for you to provide production rates and disappearance times and measures of precision

I hope this helps you.
